strengths: Tackles a practically important and underexplored setting: zero-shot anomaly generation with no anomalous samples and no fine-tuning, which better matches real deployment constraints than the dominant few-shot fine-tuning paradigm.

The core idea of contrasting two synchronized diffusion branches (normal vs. anomaly prompt) and accumulating per-step denoising deltas to build an image-specific localization mask is intuitive and well-motivated, extending single-step contrastive masking ideas (e.g., DiffEdit) to a trajectory-accumulation formulation suited to fine local defects.

The overall pipeline is coherent, combining warm-start initialization, coarse-to-fine mask refinement, token-level prompt refinement, and spatially-biased cross-attention in a complementary way, with each component individually ablated both qualitatively and quantitatively (Table 3, Fig. 4-5).

Reasonably comprehensive comparison against representative few-shot (DFMGAN, AnomalyDiffusion, AnoGen) and zero-shot (AnomalyAny, DRAEM/Crop-Paste) baselines on generation quality (IS, IC-LPIPS) and downstream detection (image/pixel AUROC and AP) on MVTec AD.
Demonstrates qualitative generalization to unseen, non-MVTec categories, supporting the cross-domain transfer claim central to the zero-shot motivation.
Honest discussion of limitations (evaluation protocol gaps, limited controllability, inability to model logical/abstract defects) rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the method largely recombines established techniques (DiffEdit-style contrastive masking, SDEdit-style partial-noise warm start, Attend-and-Excite-style attention amplification) into a new pipeline rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper would benefit from a direct ablation against a straightforward DiffEdit-style single-step contrast baseline to isolate the benefit of trajectory accumulation.

Downstream detection results (Table 2) are mixed at the category level: DeltaDeno loses to AnomalyAny on several categories (e.g., capsule, grid, toothbrush, wood, transistor) and trails few-shot methods by a sizeable margin on average, which somewhat tempers the claimed 'consistent gains' framing in the abstract.

Generation-quality comparison (Table 1) is also not uniformly favorable versus AnomalyAny (e.g., capsule, leather, tile show lower IS/IC-LPIPS for the proposed method), which is not discussed in the text.

Evaluation is concentrated on MVTec AD in the main paper, with other datasets relegated to the appendix; broader cross-domain quantitative results in the main text would better substantiate the cross-category generalization claim that is central to the paper's motivation.

Realism is assessed mainly via IS and IC-LPIPS, both known to be imperfect proxies for photorealism/localization quality; a human perceptual study or MLLM-based assessment (which the authors themselves note is missing) would strengthen the realism claims.

Key hyperparameters (partial-noise ratio γ, mask thresholds τ_mid and τ_final, number of prompt-refinement iterations) appear to be manually fixed without sensitivity analysis in the main text, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns, especially since ZSAG must work without per-category tuning data.

The paper does not report inference time/compute overhead versus AnomalyAny or few-shot baselines, which is relevant given the dual-branch synchronized denoising design and multiple auxiliary modules (SAM foreground extraction, iterative prompt optimization).

strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-explored setting (zero-shot anomaly generation with no real anomalous samples or fine-tuning), motivated by a clear and valid criticism of the dominant few-shot anomaly generation paradigm.

The core idea of accumulating per-step denoising discrepancies between a normal/anomaly prompt pair (rather than a single-step attention or latent difference as in DiffEdit/AnomalyAny) to build an image-specific localization map is a reasonable and intuitively motivated extension of existing training-free editing techniques.

The paper is reasonably well organized, with an explicit algorithm box, clear notation, and an ablation section that isolates the contribution of latent-mask inpainting, attention biasing, and prompt refinement.
Qualitative figures (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5) are illustrative and the semantic-distillation anchor offers a plausible lightweight mechanism for controlling defect type/severity without training.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'consistent gains in downstream detection performance' is not well supported by Table 2: per-category results versus the main zero-shot competitor (AnomalyAny) are actually worse in a substantial number of categories (e.g., cable 70.9 vs 89.2 AUC_i, capsule 54.9 vs 59.4, transistor 78.8 vs 78.9/similar, zipper 80.8 vs 99.9 AUC_i), and the overall improvement is driven by a few categories while others regress; averaging masks this inconsistency and overstates the robustness of the method.

Similarly, Table 1 generation-quality numbers are mixed rather than uniformly better than AnomalyAny (e.g., leather, tile, capsule, grid are worse in IS or IC-LPIPS), undermining the claim of a clear quality improvement; IS and IC-LPIPS are also weak, dataset-size-sensitive proxies for 'realism' and the paper provides no human/user study or stronger perceptual metric (e.g., FID, CLIP-based realism score) despite realism being one of the two central claimed objectives.

The method is methodologically a fairly incremental combination of existing training-free editing ingredients (DiffEdit's mask-by-prompt-contrast, SDEdit's partial-noise warm start, Attend-and-Excite/Prompt-to-Prompt-style attention biasing, blended-latent-diffusion inpainting); the delta-accumulation-over-steps and token-level embedding refinement are the main novel elements, but the paper does not clearly ablate or justify why accumulating deltas across many steps is superior to the single-step contrast used in DiffEdit/AnomalyAny beyond qualitative figures.

No runtime/efficiency comparison is provided, despite explicitly criticizing AnomalyAny for 'slow iterative inference' as a motivation; without quantitative latency/throughput numbers this comparative claim is unsubstantiated.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on a single benchmark (MVTec AD) in the main paper, with other datasets relegated to supplementary material not included here, limiting assessment of the claimed 'cross-category and cross-domain generalization.'

Key hyperparameters (tstart/γ=0.3, mask thresholds 0.6 and 0.35, loss weights λ and η, number of prompt-refinement iterations) are reported as fixed defaults without sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness and the amount of per-dataset tuning needed for a method claimed to be 'training-free' and broadly applicable.

The downstream detection protocol (training a simple U-Net purely on 100 synthetic images per category, no real anomalies) is non-standard relative to common AD evaluation practices and is not clearly justified or compared against a standard one-class/AD-model protocol, making it harder to judge the practical utility of the generated anomalies for real detector training pipelines.

No code is currently available (promised for the future), and several implementation details (e.g., SAM integration specifics, exact prompt sets per category, smoothing/cleaning of the delta map) are not fully specified, which limits reproducibility given the complexity of the pipeline.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical limitation of prior anomaly-generation work: the paper correctly identifies that few-shot anomaly generation (FSAG) requires real anomalous samples, which contradicts the motivation for generation in the first place, and targets the more useful zero-shot setting.

The core idea of delta-denoising attribution (contrasting per-step denoiser outputs of a normal-prompt and anomaly-prompt branch under a shared schedule to build an image-specific localization mask) is a reasonable and relatively novel adaptation of DiffEdit-style mask derivation to the anomaly domain, going beyond low-resolution cross-attention masks used by AnomalyAny.

The additional components (normal-reference guided initialization, token-level prompt refinement with anomaly-semantic distillation and context alignment, spatially-biased cross-attention) are individually simple and well-motivated, and the paper provides both qualitative (Fig. 4-5) and quantitative (Table 3) ablations showing each module's contribution.

Experiments cover generation quality (IS/IC-LPIPS), downstream detection utility (AUROC/AP at image and pixel level), and qualitative comparisons on both MVTec AD and unseen categories, which is a reasonably comprehensive evaluation for the claimed contribution type.

The paper is transparent about the unfair comparison with FSAG methods that leak test-set anomalies during fine-tuning, and appropriately frames AnomalyAny as the primary competitor, which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.

The controllability aspect (steering defect type/severity through the descriptive anchor in Lanom) is a nice added capability that few zero-shot generation methods offer, illustrated convincingly in Fig. 5.
weaknesses: Downstream detection results are mixed rather than uniformly better than the main ZSAG baseline: several categories (e.g., cable, capsule, grid, toothbrush, transistor, zipper) show DeltaDeno underperforming AnomalyAny on AUCi/APi, and pixel-level AP averages are lower than even AnoGen/AnoDiff (though those leak test data). The paper's narrative slightly understates this category-level variance.

The method has many hyperparameters (γ, τmid, τfinal, β, λ, η, step size αt, number of prompt-refinement iterations) whose sensitivity is not analyzed; without a hyperparameter/robustness study, reproducibility and generalization to new domains beyond MVTec-like textures remain uncertain despite the promise of code release.

Only one true zero-shot baseline (AnomalyAny) is compared against; the ZSAG literature landscape is still small, but the empirical claims of "zero-shot SOTA" would be more convincing with additional zero-shot or training-free baselines (e.g., simple DiffEdit/SDEdit adaptations) to isolate how much benefit comes from the anomaly-specific design versus generic mask-guided editing.

No computational cost / inference-time comparison is provided, even though the method runs two synchronized diffusion branches plus iterative prompt-refinement optimization, attention biasing, and SAM-based foreground extraction — this added overhead relative to AnomalyAny or single-branch methods is not quantified.

Evaluation metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS) are relatively weak proxies for photorealism/localization quality, and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this; no user study or MLLM-based assessment is included to substantiate the qualitative realism claims quantitatively.

Results on datasets beyond MVTec AD are deferred entirely to the appendix (not provided here), limiting the ability to judge cross-domain generalization claims made prominently in the abstract and introduction from the main text alone.

The technical novelty relative to DiffEdit (contrasting source/target prompts under shared schedule to derive an edit mask) is somewhat incremental; the paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of what is fundamentally new in the attribution mechanism versus adapting an existing editing paradigm to a new application.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated setting (true zero-shot anomaly generation without fine-tuning or real anomalous samples), clearly distinguishing itself from FSAG approaches that leak label information from target anomalies.

The proposed pipeline (delta-denoising attribution from two synchronized branches, mid-trajectory mask extraction, late-stage mask-guided inpainting, token-level prompt refinement, and spatially-biased cross-attention) is a coherent, well-engineered combination of ideas that is clearly described with equations and an algorithm box, aiding reproducibility.

Extensive empirical evaluation across MVTec AD and VisA, with comparisons to multiple ZSAG and FSAG baselines (DRAEM, DFMGAN, AnomalyDiffusion, AnoGen, AnomalyAny, AnoStyler), plus generation-quality metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS) and downstream detection metrics (AUROC/AP at image and pixel level).

Thorough ablations: module-wise ablation, threshold sensitivity (quantitative and qualitative), SAM dependence, runtime/memory comparison, and backbone generalization (SD1.5 vs FLUX), showing the framework is largely backbone-agnostic.

Commendable transparency in the appendix critically discussing limitations of current ZSAG evaluation protocols (IC-LPIPS anchored on real defects, entanglement of detector choice with generator quality, lack of mask-quality metrics), which strengthens the credibility of the submission rather than overselling results.
Efficiency analysis shows the method is substantially faster and more memory-efficient than a leading ZSAG baseline (AnomalyAny), which is relevant for practical deployment.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is largely combinatorial: the core delta/contrast-based mask extraction closely follows DiffEdit, attention biasing echoes Attend-and-Excite/Prompt-to-Prompt, and normal-reference initialization is a SDEdit-style warm start; the paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond assembling and adapting these known mechanisms for the anomaly-generation setting.

Downstream detection gains are inconsistent across categories (Table 2/3): DeltaDeno(SD1.5) underperforms AnomalyAny or AnoStyler on several categories (e.g., capsule, transistor, wood, zipper on MVTec; several VisA categories), which weakens the claim in the abstract of 'consistent gains'—the text should more carefully characterize where and why the method underperforms.

The headline improvement in Table 2/3 appears to come mainly from switching to the stronger FLUX backbone rather than from the proposed algorithmic contributions, since DeltaDeno(SD1.5) is only marginally better than AnoStyler on average; this raises the concern that the method's own contribution (beyond backbone choice) is modest.

No direct quantitative evaluation of mask quality against ground-truth anomaly masks (e.g., mask IoU/Dice), despite the paper's emphasis on 'precise masks' as a key selling point; mask precision is only assessed indirectly through downstream detection or qualitatively, which the authors themselves acknowledge as a shortcoming of the field but do not fully remedy.

Downstream evaluation trains a single fixed U-Net segmentation model from scratch per category using only synthetic data, which may not reflect real-world detector choices and could confound generator quality with this particular (relatively weak) detector architecture, an issue the authors flag in the discussion but do not empirically address with alternative detectors.

Several hyperparameters (β=4, λ=0.5, η=4, γ=0.3, thresholds 0.6/0.35) appear to be manually tuned defaults with limited principled justification or per-category adaptation, and the paper notes optimal thresholds vary by category yet still adopts one fixed global setting.

Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., 'great generation' in the abstract, some grammatically awkward sentences, dense notation) and reliance on external tools (SAM) for foreground priors add a dependency that, while ablated, slightly complicates the 'fully training-free, dependency-light' narrative.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: generating anomalies without any real defect samples or fine-tuning, which is a genuine limitation of prior FSAG pipelines.

The core idea of contrasting two synchronized denoising branches (normal vs. anomaly prompt) and accumulating per-step latent discrepancies into a localization map is a sensible extension of DiffEdit-style mask derivation, combined with practical engineering (normal-reference initialization, late-stage inpainting, token-level prompt refinement, spatially-biased cross-attention) that is reasonably well motivated and ablated.

Fairly extensive empirical work: generation-quality metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS), downstream detection on two datasets (MVTec AD, VisA), both SD1.5 and FLUX backbones, qualitative visualizations across many categories, and a battery of appendix ablations (SAM dependence, runtime/memory, threshold sensitivity).
The runtime/memory comparison (≈10s/10GB vs. 67s/32GB for AnomalyAny) is a meaningful practical advantage if accurate.

The appendix's self-critical discussion of evaluation protocol limitations for ZSAG (IC-LPIPS anchored on real clusters, confounding of generator and detector quality, lack of mask-pair evaluation) is a thoughtful and honest contribution that could benefit the field, though it also implicitly undercuts confidence in the paper's own headline metrics.
weaknesses: The headline downstream-detection results for the method as actually proposed (SD1.5) are not convincingly superior to prior ZSAG baselines: DeltaDeno (SD1.5) underperforms AnomalyAny or AnoStyler on many individual categories and metrics (e.g., capsule AUCi 54.9 vs 59.4/80.9; cable AUCi 70.9 vs 44.1/62.0 vs AP much lower; transistor, zipper, grid all lower), and the mean gains over AnoStyler are marginal or mixed (APi lower: 91.3 vs 91.5; AUCp only slightly higher). The strong overall claims in the abstract/intro ("great generation, realism and consistent gains") are not well supported by the per-category evidence.

Much of the reported overall improvement comes from switching the backbone to FLUX.1-dev rather than from the proposed algorithmic contributions; since FLUX is a substantially stronger, more recent generator than SD1.5 (used by all baselines), this backbone swap confounds the comparison and makes it hard to attribute gains to the proposed delta-denoising/prompt-refinement/attention-biasing mechanisms versus the generator upgrade.

The comparison with FSAG methods (Table 5) reveals a large residual gap, especially in pixel-level AP (58.4/50.0 for AnoDiff/AnoGen vs. 30.5/41.5 for DeltaDeno, roughly half), undermining the claim of "precise" localization and suggesting the zero-shot masks are considerably less accurate spatially than few-shot counterparts, despite the paper's Fig. 1 claiming "Precision: √" on par with few-shot methods.

No direct evaluation of generated mask quality against ground-truth defect masks (e.g., IoU/Dice on MVTec pixel-level annotations for synthesized-vs-real correspondence); mask quality is only inferred indirectly through downstream detector AUROC/AP, which conflates generator quality with detector architecture/training choices (an issue the paper itself acknowledges in the appendix but does not resolve).

Realism is assessed only via Inception Score, a metric poorly suited to small, localized texture-level defects on narrow industrial categories (not ImageNet-like diversity), and no human/user study of realism is provided, despite this being a common and more convincing protocol in prior anomaly-generation literature (e.g., AnomalyDiffusion, DefectFill).

Results show high sensitivity to the two threshold hyperparameters (Table 6), with an "optimal" fixed setting (0.6/0.35) applied uniformly across very heterogeneous categories; this raises concerns about robustness and the fairness of reporting a single tuned operating point as the main result.

Code is not yet released (placeholder in abstract), and several implementation choices (threshold selection, description-prompt phrasing per category, λ, η, β) appear hand-tuned, raising reproducibility concerns for a training-free method whose behavior depends heavily on these settings.

The technical novelty is largely a combination of existing techniques (DiffEdit-style contrastive masking, SDEdit-style partial noising, Attend-and-Excite-style attention biasing/token steering) adapted to the AG setting; the paper would benefit from more clearly delineating what is genuinely novel versus incremental integration.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored setting (fully zero-shot anomaly generation, no fine-tuning, no real anomalous samples) and clearly motivates why FSAG contradicts the scarcity premise it is meant to solve.

The core technical idea—accumulating per-step denoising discrepancies between paired normal/anomaly diffusion branches to build an image-specific localization map—is a reasonably novel and well-motivated instantiation of DiffEdit-style contrastive attribution adapted to the anomaly-generation problem, combined with sensible auxiliary mechanisms (normal-reference warm start, token-level prompt refinement, spatially-biased cross-attention).

Extensive empirical evaluation: generation-quality metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS), downstream detection on two benchmarks (MVTec AD, VisA) at both image and pixel level, comparisons against both FSAG and ZSAG baselines, qualitative comparisons on unseen categories, and demonstration of backbone-agnosticism by porting the method to FLUX with further gains.

Thorough ablations covering each proposed module (context alignment, attention biasing, latent inpainting, prompt refinement) both qualitatively and via downstream detection, plus threshold sensitivity analysis and a SAM-dependence ablation showing the method remains functional without SAM.
Practical considerations are addressed: runtime/memory comparison against AnomalyAny and AnoStyler shows DeltaDeno is substantially more efficient than the primary ZSAG baseline.

Commendable self-critical discussion (Appendix D) of the limitations of current IS/IC-LPIPS and downstream-AD evaluation protocols for zero-shot generation, and explicit acknowledgment of remaining limitations (limited fine-grained controllability, inability to produce logical/abstract anomalies).
weaknesses: Quantitative gains over the main ZSAG baseline (AnomalyAny) with the default SD1.5 backbone are inconsistent and often marginal or negative at the pixel level for individual categories (e.g., cable, capsule, screw in Table 2), and the headline improvements are largely driven by switching to the more powerful FLUX.1-dev backbone rather than isolating the benefit of the proposed delta-denoising mechanism itself under a matched-backbone comparison with baselines.

The paper itself argues (Appendix D.1) that IS/IC-LPIPS are poorly suited to judging zero-shot anomaly generation quality, yet these are still used as the primary quantitative realism/diversity metrics in the main results (Table 1) without an alternative, leaving the central 'realism' claim only qualitatively (Fig. 3) and not quantitatively well supported.

The method involves several sensitive hyperparameters (γ, two mask thresholds T1/T2, attention-bias strength β, prompt-refinement λ and step size η) that, despite being fixed to one default configuration across categories, show non-trivial performance swings in the threshold ablation (Table 6), suggesting some fragility/tuning burden that is somewhat at odds with the 'training-free, plug-and-play' framing.

The token-level prompt refinement performs gradient-based optimization of the anomaly embedding at inference time; while lightweight, this is a form of test-time optimization that slightly complicates the strict 'training-free' claim and is not clearly distinguished from a brief fine-tuning step in terms of reproducibility (number of iterations, convergence criteria are not specified).

Generation and detection results rely on a single normal reference image per category (one-shot generation source), and no variance/seed analysis is reported, making it hard to assess the stability of the reported gains against sampling noise in mask thresholding and diffusion generation.

Comparisons to few-shot methods (Table 5) are informative but the paper does not report any controlled setting where FSAG methods are also given only the same amount of downstream compute/backbone as DeltaDeno-FLUX, so the 'closely rivaling' claim is only loosely substantiated.
